BPA is a weak estrogenic environmental endocrine disrupting chemical (ED) which is debated whether B PA concentrations within the average human internal exposure are toxic to the developing male reproductive tract.
BPA is a potent inhibitor of human fetal Leydig cell testosterone production and insulin like 3 secretion, and that this action is not mediated by estrogen receptor alpha.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel, non-invasive, and highly sensitive method for the detection of the most common androgenic steroid hormone, testosterone.
the study of the molecular mechanisms underlying male reproductive alterations.
the effects of endocrine-disrupting compounds on the human fetal testis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of BPA is not negligible and that the current exposure of the human population to BPA may be of concern.

human fetal Leydig cell functions are affected by BPA concentrations as high as 10 7 to 10 8M, while rodent fetal Leydig cell are not affected at these concentrations and that the signaling pathways for BPA and DES are different and involve ERa in the case of DES, but not for BPA.
the effects of BPA and DES are species specific and that the effects of the two compounds are mediated by different signaling pathways.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
fetal Leydig cells are a sensitive target of environmental ED and that BPA is a specific ED which does not involve the classical estrogen receptor pathway.
BPA is a potent endocrine disruptor that is capable of disrupting fetal Leydig cells at low concentration.
BPA and DES have differential effects on human, rat and mouse fetal Leydig cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of human fetal testis cultures is essential to assess human risk and that BPA concentrations as high as 10 5 to 10 6 are required to exert a negative effect on human fetal testis steroidogenesis.
BPA has a deleterious impact on fetal Leydig function at concentrations which are close to the ones found in the general human population.
BPA may be a threat to human health at concentrations lower than those currently considered safe.
